The Lattice Boltzmann Method (LBM) is proposed as an alternative numerical approach for electromagnetic scattering.
The method is validated over a wide range of size parameters, covering Rayleigh, Mie, and geometric optics regimes.
LBM results are benchmarked against analytical Mie theory for perfect electrically conducting (PEC) and dielectric circular cylinders.
For dielectric cylinders, comparisons are performed over a broad range of relative permittivities to assess accuracy across different material contrasts.
Scattering from dielectric spheres is compared with exact Mie solutions, showing excellent agreement.
A hexagonal dielectric cylinder is investigated to assess performance for non-canonical geometries, with results validated against the Discretized Mie-Formalism (DMF).
The study provides the first systematic benchmarking of LBM for electromagnetic scattering in one-, two-, and three-dimensional configurations.
The LBM scheme is second-order accurate in both space and time, comparable to the Finite-Difference Time-Domain (FDTD) method.
The D3Q7 lattice is used for the LBM formulation, with distribution functions for electric and magnetic fields.
Macroscopic fields are reconstructed from the zeroth-order moments of the distribution functions.
Open boundary conditions are applied to suppress spurious reflections at the domain boundaries.
The near-to-far-field (NTFF) transformation is used to compute far-field observables from near-field data.
The scattering width (SW) and radar cross section (RCS) are the main scattering observables computed.
The maximum deviation between LBM results and analytical solutions for the planar interface problem is close to 1%.
For the same error level, LBM requires about three times fewer lattice points than FDTD.
The incident plane wave for cylinder scattering simulations is transverse magnetic (TMz)-polarized.
The dielectric constant used for the dielectric cylinder in benchmarking is εr = 2.
The grid resolution for PEC circular cylinder simulations is chosen such that min{a/∆x, λ/∆x} = 50.
The computational domain size is adjusted based on the size parameter, with L/a ratios of 20, 10, and 4 for a/λ < 1, a/λ = 1, and a/λ > 1, respectively.
The LBM method is implemented in a hybrid framework using C for the core solver and Python for pre- and post-processing.
The LBM method is shown to accurately capture edge diffraction and sharp-facet effects in complex scatterers.
The study demonstrates the versatility and reliability of LBM for electromagnetic scattering problems.
The LBM method is suitable for large-scale simulations due to its efficient parallelization on modern architectures.
The LBM method is validated for both dielectric and magnetic interfaces.
The LBM method is shown to be robust for high material contrasts, with deviations close to 1%.
